Analytical stance under test: Stance 140 - NCCL algorithm and protocol selection, not the parallel axis itself, can dominate the observed tensor-parallel penalty at decode message sizes.

Common frame (applies to every stance below).
Assumptions (must be restated by the answering engineer, not inherited silently):
A1. Single node, 8 GPUs, NVLink/NVSwitch intra-node; inter-node paths only appear where a stance says so explicitly.
A2. Decode-dominant, latency-sensitive serving: the SLO is TTFT p95 and TPOT (inter-token latency) p95, never a mean.
A3. Model weights fit in aggregate HBM with at least 20% KV-cache headroom at target concurrency.
A4. Exactly one variable moves per arm: no simultaneous change of quantization, batching policy, or speculative decoding.
Mechanism, stated plainly:
- Tensor parallelism (TP) shards every layer's GEMMs. Each transformer block needs two all-reduces (after attention out-projection and after the MLP down-projection), so decode carries L * 2 * allreduce_latency of synchronous cost, where L is the layer count. TP is latency-additive in collectives but capacity- and bandwidth-multiplying: per-GPU weight bytes and per-GPU KV bytes both fall by the TP degree.
- Pipeline parallelism (PP) shards layers into stages. Per token it adds only (PP-1) small point-to-point hidden-state sends, which are cheap, but a single request serializes through all stages and the bubble fraction is (PP-1)/(micro_batches + PP-1). At low concurrency there are too few in-flight micro-batches to fill the pipeline, so PP loses badly on single-request latency.
Boundary conditions that flip the answer:
- B1. On NVLink-class fabric, small-message all-reduce latency is in the single-digit microseconds and TP up to 8 is normally latency-viable. Over PCIe-only or across nodes on RoCE/IB the same collective's latency floor rises roughly an order of magnitude and TP stops paying past TP=2 (ESTIMATE; derivation: decode all-reduce payload is hidden_size * dtype_bytes per token per layer, which is small, so the collective is latency-bound rather than bandwidth-bound and the per-hop latency floor dominates).
- B2. If the model cannot fit on one GPU, sharding is mandatory and the question reduces to which axis, not whether.
- B3. Under high, steady concurrency the PP bubble amortizes and PP becomes competitive on throughput per GPU while still losing on single-request latency.
Default recommendation: use TP inside the node up to the point where collective cost stops being repaid by reduced per-GPU memory traffic; use PP only to cross a node boundary or to fit a model TP alone cannot fit. PP is not a latency optimization.

Only values read out of named benchmark artifacts may be labelled MEASURED. This review reports no MEASURED values, because no benchmark was executed for it.

At decode, the all-reduce payload per layer is hidden_size * dtype_bytes per token, which is small enough to land in NCCL's latency-bound regime. In that regime NCCL's choice of algorithm (ring versus tree versus NVLS) and protocol (LL, LL128, Simple) changes the latency floor by a large factor, and the choice is made by an internal tuning table keyed on message size, rank count and topology. A tensor-parallel arm that looks architecturally expensive may simply have fallen off the low-latency protocol because the tuner picked a bandwidth-optimal path for a message that is not bandwidth-bound. Falsifiable hypothesis H140: pinning the collective to a latency-optimised algorithm and protocol will reduce decode all-reduce time at the tested tensor degree without changing any model-level setting, and the reduction will be larger at small tensor degree message sizes than at large prefill message sizes (ESTIMATE; derivation: LL and LL128 protocols trade payload efficiency for fewer synchronisation round-trips, which only pays when the message is below the protocol crossover, and decode payloads sit below prefill payloads by roughly the prompt-length factor). Controlled experiment: Hold model, tensor degree, batching policy and precision fixed and vary only the collective tuning: default tuner, forced latency protocol, forced tree algorithm. Capture an NCCL debug trace per arm confirming which algorithm and protocol were actually selected, rather than which was requested. Rollback gate: revert to the previously validated layout if the canary's TTFT p95, TPOT p95 or error rate breaches the pre-declared bound, regardless of any aggregate throughput gain observed.

Tensor parallelism shards the KV cache along the head dimension, so per-GPU KV bytes fall roughly with the tensor degree. Pipeline parallelism moves a small hidden-state tensor between adjacent stages once per micro-batch, whereas tensor parallelism moves an activation-sized tensor through a collective twice per layer. When the boundary being crossed is a slow link, that asymmetry is decisive: the point-to-point send survives a high-latency hop far better than a per-layer synchronous all-reduce does. The correct framing is therefore that pipeline parallelism is a tool for placing a cut on the cheapest available boundary, and its bubble cost is the price paid to avoid dragging collectives across that boundary. Hold total GPU count, model, precision and batching policy fixed. Latency percentiles are only meaningful relative to a load level and an admission policy. Without a declared operating point, raising parallel degree can appear to improve latency merely because the arm with more capacity absorbs the same offered load further from saturation. Two layouts should be compared at matched utilisation, or at matched achieved throughput under a fixed latency bound, so that the reported percentile reflects the layout rather than the distance to the knee of the queueing curve. The naive model of tensor-parallel cost treats every all-reduce as fully exposed on the critical path. Prefill cost grows superlinearly in prompt length through the attention term, while decode cost grows with generated length and with key-value cache size. A workload with a long tail of long prompts is prefill-heavy and rewards the layout that parallelises compute well; a workload of short prompts with long generations is decode-heavy and rewards the layout that minimises per-step collectives and maximises cache capacity. Do not resample the trace between arms. The capacity benefit claimed for higher tensor degree assumes freed memory is usable. In practice paged or block-based key-value allocators, activation workspaces and library-level caching allocators leave usable memory below the arithmetic remainder, and the shortfall varies with block size and request-length mix.
